title: Speculative decoding explained: Medusa, EAGLE-3 and limits
summary:
Speculative decoding makes a large language model produce text faster by letting a cheaper process guess several tokens ahead while the big model checks the guesses all at once. The original paper, from Google researchers, reports a 2X to 3X speedup on a T5-XXL model with identical outputs. Later methods such as Medusa and EAGLE-3 report larger gains, under their own test conditions.

Why one token at a time is slow

A model predicts a token, adds it to the text, and predicts the next, so the steps are strictly sequential. The expensive part is moving data. According to the Medusa paper, each decoding step moves the full set of model parameters out of GPU memory, so the chip waits on data and most of its compute sits idle. Scoring several candidate tokens in one pass costs little extra, because the parameters are read once for the whole group.

title: TypeScript unused exports: what 52 popular TS repos carry, and how to clean yours with Knip
summary:
TL;DR

  • Knip finds unused files, unused exports and unused dependencies in JavaScript and TypeScript projects by following imports from your entry points, and npx knip runs it with no config.
  • In repowise's index of 48 popular TypeScript repos (1,000+ GitHub stars), unused exports (5,759) outnumber files flagged as unreachable (2,189) more than 2 to 1.
  • tsc's noUnusedLocals does not catch unused exports, because it checks one file at a time.
  • Clean up in this order: delete unused files, remove unused dependencies, run knip --fix --fix-type exports, then delete what tsc now reports as unused.

title: Telegram token in VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_? It's in your bundle
summary:
If your site was built with Lovable, or with anything else on Vite, or it's a Next.js app on Vercel, and its contact form sends messages to Telegram, look at what the bot token variable is called. If it's VITE_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN or NEXT_PUBLIC_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, the token is in the JavaScript that every visitor downloads. Your .env file stays private. The build copies the value out of it and into the public bundle anyway.

Both frameworks say this in their docs. Lovable's page on secrets says "Anything prefixed with VITE_ is a build-time, browser-exposed value." The Next.js docs say a NEXT_PUBLIC_ value "will be inlined into any JavaScript sent to the browser."

title: Bliki: Generated Glossary
summary:
When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances.

The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations generate enough text to do the job.
